mcqs.question: Bayes' theorem is derived by equating two expressions for which quantity?
options: P(A) alone
P(A∩B), expressed two ways via the conditional probability definition
P(A) + P(B)
P(A) / P(B)
mcqs.explanation: Both P(A|B)P(B) and P(B|A)P(A) equal P(A∩B) by the definition of conditional probability — setting them equal and rearranging is the entire derivation of Bayes' theorem.

mcqs.question: In Bayes' theorem vocabulary, what does the 'posterior' represent?
options: The belief held before any evidence is seen
The updated belief after incorporating the evidence
The raw evidence itself
A normalizing constant with no interpretive meaning
mcqs.explanation: The posterior, P(A|B), is exactly the updated belief after folding in evidence B — it's the output of Bayesian updating, as opposed to the prior P(A), which is the belief held beforehand.

mcqs.question: In the 1%-prevalence, 99%-accurate medical test example, why is P(disease | positive) only 50%, not 99%?
options: The test is actually only 50% accurate
Because the disease is rare, false positives from the large healthy population roughly match the true positives from the small sick population
The calculation given in the example is wrong
50% is just a coincidence with no explanation
mcqs.explanation: With only 1% prevalence, the 99% healthy population still generates a comparable number of false positives (1% of a huge group) to the true positives from the small sick group — that's why base rate, not just test accuracy, determines the posterior.

mcqs.question: The base-rate fallacy specifically describes ignoring which quantity?
options: The test's sensitivity (true positive rate)
P(A), the prior probability of the condition before any test evidence
The sample size of the study
The test's cost
mcqs.explanation: The base-rate fallacy is specifically about anchoring on the test's accuracy while ignoring how common the condition is beforehand (P(A), the prior/base rate) — that prior is exactly what a naive intuitive estimate leaves out.

mcqs.question: What assumption makes Naive Bayes 'naive,' and why is it made despite usually being false?
options: That all classes are equally likely a priori
That features are conditionally independent given the class, which makes an otherwise intractable joint-probability estimate tractable
That there is only one feature per data point
That the data has no noise
mcqs.explanation: Assuming conditional independence collapses an otherwise exponentially large joint-probability estimation problem into a product of simple per-feature likelihoods — the assumption is usually technically wrong, but the resulting classifier is cheap to estimate and works well in practice anyway.

mcqs.question: A DNA match has a 1-in-a-million false-positive rate. The prosecutor's fallacy would incorrectly conclude what?
options: That the defendant is definitely guilty
That there's a 1-in-a-million chance the defendant is innocent, treating P(evidence|innocent) as if it were P(innocent|evidence)
That DNA evidence is never reliable
That the base rate doesn't matter for any probability calculation
mcqs.explanation: The fallacy conflates P(evidence|innocent) — a small number — with P(innocent|evidence), ignoring how many people were ever in the suspect pool (the prior/base rate); a correct Bayesian calculation accounts for that pool size explicitly.
